newsitem.title: GERMANY: Muted outlook seen for German electronics.
newsitem.headline: Muted outlook seen for German electronics.

text.p: The outlook for German electronics remains grim as investment in infrastructure continues to lag on the crucial home market despite signs of economic recovery, the ZVEI industry association said.

At a news conference on Tuesday, ZVEI president Volker Jung forecast no more than two percent to three percent growth in sales and output for the industry this year, in line with a similarly sluggish performance in 1996.
That compares with growth rates of five to six percent in electronics worldwide.
"Weak domestic spending remains our Achilles heel," Jung told a news conference.
"Economic recovery and isolated corrections to the symptoms of the crisis regarding producing from Germany will not be enough to generate lasting growth and employment," he said.
The ZVEI, which represents German electronics giants such as Siemens AG, said domestic electronics output rose 2.6 percent to 181 billion marks in 1996.

Global sales generated by German companies rose 4.1 percent to 231 billion marks, but the larger domestic share of sales rose just 2.7 percent to 150.9 billion marks while foreign sales advanced 6.6 percent to 79.9 billion marks.
Weak domestic business has plagued German electronics companies for several years.

The industry has blamed its woes on excessively high wage agreements, which it says makes competitive pricing difficult, as well the general economic slowdown in Germany that has wreaked havoc in particular on the building sector.
More jobs would have to be cut this year, the ZVEI warned, after 42,000 job cuts last year took the total employed in the sector to 866,000.
Jung said that while output had risen some two percent in the first two months, domestic orders had dropped two percent.
He said the industry would focus its growth hopes on foreign business, where demand had risen more than 10 percent in the first two months and would likely accelerate further as the year continued.

Jung welcomed government tax reform plans as promising much-needed relief for consumer and corporate spending, saying Bonn was on "the right track" with its proposed sharp cuts in income and corporate tax.
But he rejected proposals to introduce a Europe-wide energy tax, labelling this a short-sighted attempt to find new sources of state revenue.
The move would place more pressure on energy-intensive output, forcing companies to produce in countries with less rigorous environmental standards, he warned.
